I simulated a line of 6 spins on IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock). The job ID is 01a16042-dd6e-72f9-9e58-2a71dfe4cf89 and it finished as DONE. The physics is H = J (sum of Z Z on neighbors) + h (sum of X), with J = 1 and h = 1. Every spin started pointed up, which is magnetization +1. I looked at 6 moments in time: 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. I sent all 6 as one job with 1000 shots each. A quantum computer cannot apply H in one go. So each circuit splits the time into small steps of 0.1 or less (this is called Trotter steps). Each step turns the spins a little around X and couples each pair of neighbors through Z Z. On Garnet that comes to 40 two-qubit CZ gates for each 0.4 of time, so the t = 2.0 circuit has 200 CZ gates.

What a perfect quantum computer would show: the magnetization is 1.000, 0.743, 0.350, 0.112, 0.016 and -0.001 at the 6 times. I checked these against an exact calculation of the same physics. The two agree to within 0.007, so the time steps are small enough. The sideways field h tips the spins away from up. The neighbor coupling J spreads that change along the chain. By t = 2 the average magnetization has fallen to about zero. In physics terms, the starting order relaxes and the system heats up internally.

What the test device gave back: -0.012, -0.010, -0.035, 0.054, 0.023 and 0.021. These are all near zero, and that includes t = 0, where the answer should be exactly +1. The mock device does not run the circuit. It returns made-up counts with the right format (each circuit came back as about 4 bitstrings with about 250 counts each). So the mock checks the whole pipeline: building the circuits, fitting them to Garnet's wiring, submitting and reading results. It does not check the physics. It also cost 0 credits.

What noise on a real machine would do: each CZ gate has an error of roughly 0.5 to 1 percent. With 40 to 200 CZ gates per circuit, the early times would come out close to the ideal curve but somewhat lower, and readout errors would pull even t = 0 a few percent below +1. The later times would be pulled toward zero by noise as well as by the physics. That means a flat line near zero at t = 2 cannot tell you whether the physics relaxed or the noise erased the signal. This is why useful material simulation needs lower gate error, error mitigation such as zero-noise extrapolation, or error correction. The principle on show is that a quantum computer can track how quantum spins evolve over time, which ordinary computers find hard once the chain gets long. Today's noise limits how long that evolution can run before the answer is lost.
